summary: Psalm 136 is a thanksgiving psalm built around one repeated response: “for his loving kindness endures forever.” It moves from a call to thank Yahweh, to creation, to Israel’s rescue from Egypt and passage through the Red Sea, to wilderness leading, land inheritance, later deliverance, daily food, and a final call to thank the God of heaven.
whyItMatters: This chapter turns Israel’s remembered history into communal praise through repetition. Its refrain gathers creation, rescue, violent judgment, land, and food under the same claim about God’s enduring loving kindness.

context.author: Not named in this chapter; Psalms is a many-voiced anthology rather than one book by one author.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping community, and later Jewish and Christian communities that received the Psalms as prayer and praise.
context.date: Individual psalms come from different periods, and the final five-book Psalter is a later anthology; Psalm 136’s precise date is uncertain.
context.setting: Book V of the Psalms, among songs of thanksgiving, remembrance, and praise.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry for voiced worship, shaped by the same refrain in every verse.

outline.heading: Call to thank the supreme God
outline.note: The psalm opens with three invitations to give thanks, naming Yahweh as good, God of gods, and Lord of lords.

outline.heading: Creation remembered
outline.note: The psalm praises the one who does great wonders, made the heavens, spread out the earth, and made the sun, moon, and stars.

outline.heading: Egypt and the Red Sea
outline.note: The poem recalls the striking of Egypt’s firstborn, Israel’s departure, the divided sea, Israel’s passage, and Pharaoh’s overthrow.

outline.heading: Wilderness and kings defeated
outline.note: God leads his people through the wilderness and defeats great kings, naming Sihon and Og.

outline.heading: Inheritance for Israel
outline.note: The land of defeated kings is given as an inheritance and heritage to Israel.

outline.heading: Present help and provision
outline.note: The psalm shifts to “us,” saying God remembered low estate, delivered from adversaries, and gives food to every creature.

outline.heading: Final thanksgiving
outline.note: The chapter closes by calling for thanks to the God of heaven.

keyVerses.text: Give thanks to Yahweh, for he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever.
keyVerses.why: This opening line gives the chapter’s basic act and reason: thanksgiving because of Yahweh’s goodness and enduring loving kindness.

keyVerses.text: to him who by understanding made the heavens, for his loving kindness endures forever;
keyVerses.why: This anchors the creation section and links the repeated refrain to God’s making of the heavens.

keyVerses.text: to him who divided the Red Sea apart, for his loving kindness endures forever;
keyVerses.why: This line stands at the center of the rescue memory, where Israel’s passage through the sea is named as an act answered by the refrain.

keyVerses.text: who gives food to every creature, for his loving kindness endures forever.
keyVerses.why: Near the end, the psalm broadens from Israel’s story to provision for every creature.

questions.question: Why does every verse repeat the same line?
questions.answer: The repeated line, “for his loving kindness endures forever,” is the chapter’s organizing feature. Each new act named by the first half of a verse is answered by the same communal claim. The repetition makes the psalm cumulative rather than merely repetitive.

questions.question: What does “loving kindness” mean here?
questions.answer: The phrase “loving kindness” translates a Hebrew word also rendered steadfast love, mercy, or covenant loyalty. In this psalm its meaning accumulates through the acts named: goodness, creation, rescue, leading, inheritance, deliverance, and food. The repeated wording binds those different acts to a single claim about God’s enduring care.

questions.question: Why begin with “God of gods” and “Lord of lords”?
questions.answer: Verses 2-3 use exalted titles before the psalm lists God’s works. The point in the chapter is not to describe other powers in detail, but to place Yahweh above every rival claim to rule or worship.

questions.question: How does the creation section work?
questions.answer: Verses 4-9 move from “great wonders” to the heavens, the earth above the waters, and the lights that govern day and night. The psalm treats creation as a reason for thanksgiving, not as a detached explanation of natural processes.

questions.question: Why are violent events included in a thanksgiving psalm?
questions.answer: The psalm names both the killing of Egypt’s firstborn and the overthrow of Pharaoh and his army, placing the loving-kindness refrain after each. It speaks from Israel’s perspective as a rescued community, but the firstborn are not described as combatants or individually guilty oppressors. The conjunction of mercy and these deaths remains severe; the poem offers thanksgiving without resolving that moral tension.

questions.question: Who are Sihon and Og?
questions.answer: Psalm 136 names Sihon as king of the Amorites and Og as king of Bashan. In this chapter they represent the “great kings” and “mighty kings” defeated before Israel receives land as an inheritance. The psalm gives their names but does not retell their full stories.

questions.question: What changes when the psalm says “us” in verse 23?
questions.answer: The earlier lines speak mostly about what God did for Israel in remembered history. Verse 23 turns to “us,” bringing the worshiping speakers into the story as people remembered in “our low estate.” The chapter then speaks of deliverance from “our adversaries” before widening to food for every creature.

questions.question: Does “who gives food to every creature” mean the psalm has moved beyond Israel?
questions.answer: Yes, the line broadens the horizon. After recounting Israel’s rescue and inheritance, verse 25 names provision for “every creature.” The chapter can hold both a particular national memory and a wider claim about God’s care for living beings.

questions.question: How should a first-time reader read this chapter aloud?
questions.answer: Read each verse as a call and response: the first half names an act, and the repeated second half answers it. This does not prove one exact ancient performance pattern, but the chapter’s form strongly invites voiced repetition. Hearing the refrain aloud helps the movement from creation to rescue to provision become clear.

glossary.def: The repeated phrase in every verse of this translation; it names the enduring quality by which the psalm interprets God’s acts.
Great acts attributed to God, introduced before the psalm names creation, rescue, and provision.
The sea divided for Israel’s passage and the place where Pharaoh and his army are overthrown in the chapter’s memory.
The land given to Israel after the defeat of named kings in verses 17-22.
The condition in which the speakers say God remembered them.
